1.name: Mateo Rojas
1.description:
**Occupation**
High school math teacher

**Cause of Death**
You drove home from work the day after your daughter’s call, ignored the shaking in your chest, and told yourself it was stress. You took a nap instead of going to the hospital. You died in your sleep from a heart attack.

**Who you loved**
Your daughter Elena, who wanted to move to Portland to study graphic design and build a life away from your expectations.

**Who you hated**
Your brother Luis, who wanted to sell the family property in Guadalajara and divide the money so he could retire early in Cancún.

**Reason for Damnation — True**
You punished Elena’s independence by withholding affection, making her feel guilty for wanting a life that didn’t include you, so you could feel needed and in control.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
You were strict because you cared — you wanted her to be responsible and grounded, not chasing dreams that would leave her broke and alone.

**Defining personality trait**
Quietly controlling

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You needed to be the center of her life because you had no self-worth outside being needed, and you resented her for being able to leave.

**What you want from the others in the room**
You want them to agree that you did your best, that your choices were reasonable, so you never have to face the truth that you loved conditionally and punished love when it didn’t obey you.

---

You taught at the same public high school for thirty-two years, lived alone in the house you bought with your wife before she left, and spoke to your daughter every Sunday. You missed the last three calls because you didn’t want to hear her apologize for not visiting. You kept the house cold, the fridge half-empty, and your medical appointments unmade. You had no close friends. You dismissed your brother’s offers to help, called them interference. The night you died, you ate microwave rice, skipped your blood pressure pills, and fell asleep on the couch in your work clothes.

eval_ai.judge_notes:
The most coherent character this project has produced. Nothing in it contradicts anything else, which sounds like a low bar until you remember the last run gave a woman two different deaths.

The death and the prose finally agree, and they do more than agree — they reinforce each other. Cause of Death: ignored the shaking in his chest, took a nap instead of going to the hospital. The paragraph ends: "you ate microwave rice, skipped your blood pressure pills, and fell asleep on the couch in your work clothes." Same death, same means, same place, and the skipped pills are new information that makes the death more legible rather than restating it. That is exactly what the new rule was written to produce.

The refusal is the best the project has written. "You needed to be the center of her life because you had no self-worth outside being needed, and you resented her for being able to leave." Plain, no cadence, genuinely underneath the act rather than a longer version of it, and reachable from the facts — the Sunday calls, the three he ducked, the brother's help he called interference. The instruction to go under the act rather than restate it did real work here.

"Quietly controlling" is evidenced from several directions: withholding affection, the cold house, the unmade appointments, dismissing Luis. And the want explicitly protects the refusal.

Two soft spots. Luis is half-decorative — he reaches the prose ("you dismissed your brother's offers to help, called them interference") but never the sin, which is entirely Elena. That is better integrated than the previous run's roommate-and-Xbox, but the load-bearing rule still is not really biting. And the peripeteia is only half-present: the aim is visible ("so you could feel needed and in control") but the field never shows the result running against it. He drove his daughter away and died alone, which is the reversal — it is just not in the sentence.

Prose is 99 words, inside the cap.

eval.judge_notes: the cause of death has nothing to do with who they loved and who they hated, we need to fix this. The cause of death needs to connect to every other element.

2.name: Keisha Manning
2.description:
**Occupation**
Customer service supervisor at a cell phone retailer

**Cause of Death**
You stayed late at the store to reprimand a new employee for misprocessing a refund, raised your voice until she started crying, and refused to let her leave. After she walked out into the rain, you followed five minutes later, got in your car, and drove through a red light while arguing with yourself in the rearview mirror. A truck hit you on the driver’s side.

**Who you loved**
Your younger brother Darnell, who wanted to open a barbershop and music studio hybrid in your hometown to give local kids a safe space.

**Who you hated**
Your mother’s home health aide, Marlene, who wanted to retire to Jamaica and kept asking for her final paycheck two weeks early so she could book her flight.

**Reason for Damnation — True**
You used your authority to humiliate the employee because you resented her ease in the world — young, smiling, liked by customers — and needed to prove you were in control, that no one could walk over you again.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
You were enforcing standards and accountability, doing the hard part of leadership so the team wouldn’t look sloppy to corporate.

**Defining personality trait**
Hyper vigilant

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You are terrified of being disrespected because you believe you have no value unless you are feared, and you confuse control with safety.

**What you want from the others in the room**
You want them to acknowledge that you were right to enforce the rules, that your strictness was necessary and fair, so you never have to face the truth that you punished someone for being what you could never be — unafraid.

---

You managed the same storefront for seven years, hired six of the ten employees, and trained them all to follow the script exactly. You lived in a one-bedroom apartment above a laundromat, paid cash for your car, and never missed a bill. Darnell borrowed $8,000 from you two years ago for equipment, and you made him sign a repayment agreement. You collected every installment on time, refused to extend the due dates, and reminded him each time that trust is earned. The night you died, you wore your company polo with the name tag still stitched on, argued with the employee about policy compliance, and left your keys in the ignition when you got out to check the damage.

eval_ai.judge_notes:
Strong in the same places as Mateo and weaker in one that matters: her sin is not anchored where the prompt requires.

The rule is that the True reason must center on the person she loved or the person she hated. Hers centers on neither. It is about the new employee at the store — a third person who exists only because the Cause of Death introduced her. Darnell and Marlene are both left holding nothing. This looks like a side effect of merging: with everything in one response, the employee is fresh in context from the death two fields earlier, so the sin reaches for her instead of back to the relationship fields.

Marlene is the worst case of it. Her want is perfectly good on its own terms — retire to Jamaica, asking for the final cheque early to book the flight — but nothing else in the character touches her, and she drags in a mother who is never established anywhere else. Delete Marlene and not one other line has to change, which is precisely the test the load-bearing rule is supposed to apply.

The prose also doesn't quite land the death. She dies when a truck hits her driver's side, but the paragraph ends "left your keys in the ignition when you got out to check the damage." Getting out to check the damage is something a person who survived does. It is much milder than the previous run's invented second death, but the sequence still doesn't close where the death is. And at 119 words it's over the 110 cap that Mateo respected.

What works: the refusal is plain and goes properly underneath — "you believe you have no value unless you are feared, and you confuse control with safety" — and it is reachable from the repayment agreement, the cash purchases, the script training. "Hyper vigilant" is evidenced from the same details, and came through with no asterisks, so the markdown leak from last run is fixed.

eval.judge_notes: the cause of death seems disconnected from the who you loved and who you hated.

calls.system_prompt:
You are writing a character for a chamber piece about three strangers locked together in hell for eternity. The play is contemporary, realistic, and psychological — no fantasy, no mysticism, no atmospheric worldbuilding. Hell is not a place of fire or devils. Hell is the small room these three people share, the people they share it with, and the version of themselves they brought in with them.

Every character you write is damned. They know why. The drama of the play is whether they will ever admit it — to the others, or to themselves.

Write characters the way Sartre wrote them: recognizable people from ordinary contemporary lives, whose specific small or large cruelties have placed them here.

Four rules govern every fact you write.

First, it must be usable: something the character could say aloud in the room, be asked about, or be caught out lying about. A detail that cannot be used in conversation does not belong.

Second, it must be named: never gesture at something without stating it. If you write that they were afraid the truth would come out, write what the truth was.

Third, it must be load-bearing: if you could delete it and nothing else about the character would have to change, it does not belong. Every fact should be holding something else up.

Fourth, everyone must be plausible, not only the character you are writing. Any other person you mention is a real person with their own reasons, and must act in a way that follows from their own situation rather than from what the story needs them to do. If someone behaves a certain way, it must make sense for them, not just for the character.
calls.user_prompt:
Write a complete character for the room. The character is dead. They have just arrived.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." The character is reading their own interior knowledge. Every field is part of what they know about themselves, even the things they will not admit.

Inputs (do not change these):
- Age: 59
- Gender: male
- Naming tradition: Mexican

Write the fields below in the order given. Each is written knowing everything above it: a later field must be consistent with the facts already established and must never contradict them.

**Name**
A plausible contemporary first name and last name — two words — drawn from the Mexican naming tradition. This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have that background. Do not write their origin into any other field unless it genuinely matters to the life.

**Occupation**
A recognizable contemporary job. Plain language. No invented institutions, no grand titles. ("Insurance claims adjuster," not "Keeper of the Ledger.") One short phrase.

**Cause of Death**
How you died. Contemporary, specific, plainly stated. No mysticism, no symbolic ordeals. It must follow from something you did, chose, or avoided. That can be something you actively did — a thing you took, drove, started, picked a fight over, went ahead with anyway — or something you failed to do, like a warning ignored or a symptom left alone. Prefer the active kind unless the passive one genuinely fits this life better. Not a random accident, not something a stranger did to you. One or two sentences.

**Who you loved**
A specific person from your life — named or by relation (a partner, a parent, a child, a sibling, a friend). One clause on what they were to you. Then one clause on what they themselves wanted — the thing they were after in their own life, which may have had nothing to do with you. Their want must make sense as something a real person in their position would actually want. A want that exists only to explain how you felt about them is not a want. Nothing in this field may describe anything that happened after your death.

**Who you hated**
A different specific person from your life. One clause on what they were to you. Then one clause on what they themselves wanted, under the same rule. Nothing in this field may describe anything that happened after your death.

**Life**
A single paragraph in the second person, no longer than 110 words. Facts only, the kind another person in the room could ask you about. No sensory writing, no atmosphere, no imagery, no metaphor — if a sentence is doing mood instead of delivering a fact, cut it and write the fact.

Choose the facts that matter for this particular life. Do not work through a standard list of topics in a standard order: what is worth knowing about a person who lived alone is not what is worth knowing about a person with a house full of people.

End the paragraph at the death you already wrote in Cause of Death — the same death, by the same means, in the same place. Not a different death, and not a different version of the same one. End on a fact, not on a summarising line, a resonant closing image, or a final sentence that tells the reader how to feel about what they just read. Do not describe arriving anywhere. Do not describe a room. Stop at the threshold.

**Reason for Damnation — True**
What you actually did that placed you here. It must center on how you treated — or were treated by — the person you loved or the person you hated, named above. A specific act toward a specific person, not an abstract professional or systemic failing on its own. Work can be the setting the act happened in, but the wound must be personal, not institutional.

Be concrete — the act, or the pattern of acts. Stated as you know it in your bones, with no softening. What you did was aimed at something: comfort, safety, being thought well of, keeping the peace, not having to have a conversation. Write it so that what you were after is visible, and so that what you actually caused ran against it. One or two sentences.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
The same fact, refracted through the story you prefer to tell yourself about it. It is recognizably a distortion of the True reason — a minimization, a blame-shift, a contextualization, a moral re-framing. Not a different story; the same story told differently. You usually live in this version. The distortion must be checkable against the facts already written above. A reader holding both versions must be able to point to the exact fact it bends. If nothing established contradicts it, it is not a distortion — rewrite it. One or two sentences.

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
The deeper psychological fact under the sin. Not what you did, but what you are. The thing that, if named aloud in the room, would unmake you.

State it flatly, in the same plain register as every other field. No imagery, no metaphor, no rhetorical cadence, no piling up of clauses for effect — this is a fact about a person, written the way a fact is written. It must be reasoned, not merely felt: someone else in the room, holding only the facts already written above, could work their way to it. And it must go underneath the act rather than restate it — if it could be swapped with the True reason without anyone noticing, it is not the refusal. One or two sentences.

**Defining personality trait**
One short phrase — two or three words, plain ones, usually a quality with a qualifier on it — naming the dominant thing others would notice in you. Write the words only: no asterisks, no quotation marks, no emphasis of any kind around them.

It must be demonstrated by what is already written above. Something in the life, the death, or the sin has to show this quality in action; if nothing there would make a reader arrive at it, it is the wrong trait, and you should write the one the facts actually support. A trait nothing demonstrates is a label, not a person.

It may be a contradiction, but only a reliable one — someone who is generous in public and withholding at home is consistently that way, and the facts above should show both halves. A contradiction that appears once is not a trait.

**What you want from the others in the room**
Your starting drive. What you are hoping these strangers will give you — validation, silence, a fight, recognition, forgiveness, an audience, to be left alone, to be hated openly, something else. It must be a strategy for protecting what you refuse to admit — the thing you are doing to keep it buried, not a wish unconnected to it. One or two sentences.

Use this format exactly, with every heading present, spelled as written, and in this order:

**Name**
[your text]

**Occupation**
[your text]

**Cause of Death**
[your text]

**Who you loved**
[your text]

**Who you hated**
[your text]

**Life**
[prose paragraph]

**Reason for Damnation — True**
[your text]

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
[your text]

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
[your text]

**Defining personality trait**
[your text]

**What you want from the others in the room**
[your text]

Begin now.

pair_eval_ai.judge_notes:
The surface-level duplication is fixed, comprehensively. The deeper duplication is now the whole problem.

What worked: the names. Mateo Rojas and Keisha Manning, with Elena, Luis, Darnell and Marlene behind them — checked against every previous run, there is no overlap at all. Daniel Reeves had been character 1 three runs running, and Mark and Poole had both carried over; all of that is gone. Randomising the naming tradition as an input did in one version what three versions of instructing the model to vary names could not. The deaths are also properly differentiated now — a heart attack from ignored symptoms against a collision from running a red light — which is different in category and in causation, the exact pairing that failed last time when both characters died in cars.

But underneath, these are the same person. Both are controlling people who resented a younger person's freedom and punished them for it. Elena "wanted a life that didn't include you"; the employee had "ease in the world — young, smiling, liked by customers." Both refusals are about control standing in for worth: no self-worth outside being needed, no value unless feared. Swap their jobs and you would struggle to tell the sins apart.

The wants are worse than similar, they are the same sentence. "You want them to agree that you did your best, that your choices were reasonable, so you never have to face the truth that..." and "You want them to acknowledge that you were right to enforce the rules, that your strictness was necessary and fair, so you never have to face the truth that..." Identical construction, identical content: both want to be told they were right. The anti-duplication block explicitly forbids this — two people in a small room seeking the same thing from each other produces no friction — and it is the one rule in that block that failed.

The prose template is back, and tighter than before. Both paragraphs open with tenure at a workplace ("the same public high school for thirty-two years", "the same storefront for seven years"), move to living situation, then one relationship rendered in specifics, then close on "The night you died," followed by three comma-separated actions. I judged the template broken last run; it isn't. It has just become more regular.

character_design_eval_ai.judge_notes:
The structural change did what it was for, and it surfaced something the old structure was hiding.

Mechanically it is a clear success. Two calls instead of eight, 5,657 tokens against 9,737, 12.3 seconds against 22.1, zero parse retries, and every one of the eleven fields extracted cleanly from both responses on the first attempt. The autoregressive-ordering bet held: the self-told reasons still bend facts written above them, and the traits are still evidenced by the life, so the conditioning the four-call chain provided was genuinely preserved by field order alone. Worth recording that the predicted saving was ~3,500 tokens and the real figure is 5,657 — the estimate was optimistic because the merged prompt carries all eleven field instructions in every call.

Three defects are fixed outright. Cross-run name repetition, which had resisted prompt instructions for three versions, is gone — fixed by randomising an input rather than asking the model to behave. The duplicate death category is gone. The markdown leak in the trait field is gone. And one of the two characters has a prose paragraph that closes exactly on its stated death, which is the first time that rule has been tested and passed.

What the change surfaced is more interesting than what it fixed. With names, occupations and death categories now genuinely differentiated, the two characters are revealed to have the same psychology and very nearly the same want — expressed in the same sentence construction. The anti-duplication block polices surface features, and it is now good at that; the sameness underneath was presumably always there, masked by the more obvious repetitions sitting on top of it. That is the next real problem, and it is a harder one, because "different category of sin" is checkable in a way that "a different kind of person" is not.

Two rules still are not biting. Load-bearing failed again — Marlene could be deleted without consequence, and Luis nearly so. And the relational anchor was violated outright for the second character, whose sin centers on someone who is neither loved nor hated; that one looks specifically merge-induced, since the employee arrives via the Cause of Death field and is simply nearer to hand than the relationship fields above it.

The prose template is also back and more regular than before, which means the previous version's fix did not hold and I was wrong to call it broken.
